questions.question: Which contemporary chronicler acknowledged that Raziyya Sultan was more capable than her brothers?
questions.solution: The correct answer is __**Minhaj-us-Siraj**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** • **Minhaj-us-Siraj**, a Persian historian and chronicler of the 13th century, documented the history of the Delhi Sultanate in his famous work, the **"Tabaqat-i-Nasiri."** • In his writings, he acknowledged that **Raziyya Sultan** was more competent and capable than her brothers in handling the affairs of the state. • Raziyya Sultan, the first and only female ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, was chosen by her father, **Iltutmish**, as his successor due to her administrative skills and leadership qualities. • Minhaj-us-Siraj praised her for her intelligence, bravery, and ability to manage state affairs, which made her stand out among her contemporaries. • This acknowledgment is significant as it highlights the progressive mindset of Iltutmish and the exceptional abilities of Raziyya Sultan during a time when women were rarely seen in leadership roles.

questions.question: Who were called 'Bandagan' in Persian in Delhi Sultanate?

options.text: Military slaves purchased by the Sultan

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Military slaves purchased by the Sultan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The term **'Bandagan'** in Persian refers to **military slaves** who were purchased by the Sultans of the Delhi Sultanate.

• The Bandagan were often recruited from Central Asia or other foreign regions and served as trusted aides, administrators, and military commanders.

• These slaves were trained in military and administrative skills and were often rewarded with high ranks and positions of power.

• The Bandagan played a crucial role in ensuring the Sultan’s authority over his empire and were instrumental in maintaining a strong central administration.

• Notable examples of Bandagan include **Malik Kafur**, a prominent military commander under Alauddin Khilji, who was originally a slave.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Delhi Sultanate:** 

• The Delhi Sultanate was a Muslim kingdom that ruled over large parts of India from the **13th to 16th century**.

• It consisted of five dynasties: the Slave Dynasty, Khilji Dynasty, Tughlaq Dynasty, Sayyid Dynasty, and Lodi Dynasty.

• The Sultanate was known for its strong military and administrative system.

• **Role of Bandagan:** 

• The Bandagan were essential in the Sultan’s military campaigns and administrative tasks.

• They acted as governors, military generals, and even advisors to the Sultan.

• They were loyal to the Sultan because their status and power depended on his favor.

• **Notable Bandagan Figures:** 

• **Malik Kafur:** A military commander under Alauddin Khilji who led several successful campaigns in southern India.

• **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq:** Originally a slave who rose to become the founder of the Tughlaq Dynasty.

• **Slavery in the Delhi Sultanate:** 

• Slavery was an institutionalized practice, and slaves were often brought from foreign regions like Central Asia.

• Slaves were trained and educated to serve in administrative or military roles.

• The Sultan relied heavily on slaves for loyalty and efficiency in governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Military Slaves:** The concept of military slaves was not unique to the Delhi Sultanate; similar practices existed in other medieval Islamic states, including the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt.

• **Hierarchy:** Despite being slaves initially, many Bandagan rose to powerful positions, influencing the Sultanate’s policies and governance.

• **Cultural Impact:** The Bandagan were instrumental in spreading Persian culture and administrative practices throughout India.

• **Challenges:** Over time, the loyalty of some Bandagan diminished, leading to internal conflicts and power struggles within the Sultanate.

36:T

questions.question: Which article of the Indian Constitution mentions that "There shall be a High Court for each State"?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 214**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Article 214** of the **Indian Constitution** states that "There shall be a High Court for each State." 
• The article ensures the establishment of a High Court as the highest judicial authority at the state level, responsible for administering justice within its territorial jurisdiction. 
• It provides the framework for the existence of a High Court in each state, although Parliament has the power to establish a common High Court for two or more states as per **Article 231**. 
• High Courts in India have jurisdiction over matters such as civil, criminal, constitutional, and administrative law, among others, within their respective states. 
• Each High Court is headed by a Chief Justice, and its composition and appointment procedures are governed by the Constitution of India. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Article 124:** 
• This article deals with the establishment and composition of the **Supreme Court of India**. 
• The Supreme Court is the apex judicial body in India, and its primary role is to act as a guardian of the Constitution. 
• It comprises the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and other judges as determined by Parliament. 
• **Article 226:** 
• Under this article, High Courts have the power to issue writs (such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari) for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose. 
• This article empowers High Courts to ensure that the rule of law is upheld within their respective jurisdictions. 
• **Article 32:** 
• This article provides the right to constitutional remedies, allowing individuals to directly approach the Supreme Court for the enforcement of fundamental rights. 
• It is often referred to as the "heart and soul" of the Indian Constitution, as described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. 
• **High Courts in India:** 
• The **Calcutta High Court**, established in **1862**, is the oldest High Court in India. 
• As of **2023**, there are **25 High Courts** in India, including common High Courts for some states and union territories. 
• For example, the High Court of Punjab and Haryana is a common High Court for these two states and the union territory of Chandigarh. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Role of High Courts:** 
• High Courts are responsible for overseeing subordinate courts, including district courts, within their jurisdiction. 
• They also have the authority to hear appeals from lower courts and provide remedies for violations of legal and constitutional rights. 
• **Appointment of Judges:** 
• Judges of the High Courts are appointed by the President of India in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the respective state, and sometimes other judges of the High Court. 
• The qualifications for appointment include being a citizen of India and having at least **10 years** of experience as an advocate or a judicial officer. 
• **Jurisdiction of High Courts:** 
• They have **original jurisdiction** in matters like fundamental rights and election disputes. 
• They also have **appellate jurisdiction** over civil and criminal cases decided by subordinate courts. 
• **Significance of Article 214:** 
• This article ensures the decentralized administration of justice by establishing High Courts in states, making access to justice more efficient and localized. </ul

questions.question: The term "MOVCDNER" which is seen in news in October 2024 is related to which sector?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Agriculture**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 __ 
• **MOVCDNER** stands for **Mission Organic Value Chain Development for North Eastern Region**. It is an initiative launched by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India. 
• The program aims to promote organic farming and develop certified organic value chains in the **North Eastern Region of India** comprising eight states: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, and Tripura. 
• MOVCDNER provides support for the entire value chain including production, certification, processing, and marketing of organic produce, ensuring farmers’ access to premium markets. 
• The scheme emphasizes the cultivation of high-value crops such as spices, fruits, and vegetables, which are native to the North Eastern region and have significant export potential. 
• It is aligned with the goal of fostering sustainable agriculture and leveraging the region’s unique biodiversity to create economic opportunities for farmers. 
• MOVCDNER is implemented through clusters or Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs) to ensure better coordination, training, and financial assistance to farmers. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Organic Farming in India:** 
• Organic farming is a method of farming that avoids the use of synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, and genetically modified organisms, focusing on sustainable agricultural practices. 
• India is home to one of the largest numbers of organic producers globally, with states like **Sikkim** achieving the status of being a fully organic state. 
• Organic farming promotes soil health, biodiversity conservation, and reduction in environmental pollution. 
• **Features of MOVCDNER:** 
• The scheme provides financial assistance for activities such as organic certification, market linkages, packaging, branding, and infrastructure development. 
• Farmers under the program receive training in organic farming techniques and are supported with inputs like bio-fertilizers and bio-pesticides. 
• The program encourages the formation of **Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs)** to enhance collective bargaining and reduce transaction costs. 
• The focus is on export-oriented products such as **black pepper, turmeric, ginger, and large cardamom**, which have high demand in international markets. 
• **Government Initiatives in Agriculture:** 
• **Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY):** A scheme promoting traditional organic farming methods, introduced in 2015. 
• **National Agriculture Market (eNAM):** An online platform launched to enable farmers to sell their produce directly in transparent and competitive markets. 
• **Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana:** A crop insurance scheme protecting farmers against crop loss due to natural disasters. 
• **Challenges in Organic Farming:** 
• High initial costs for organic inputs and certification. 
• Limited awareness among farmers regarding organic farming practices. 
• Inadequate market infrastructure for organic produce. 
• Difficulty in meeting international organic standards for export purposes. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Sikkim:** Became the first fully organic state in the world in **2016**, showcasing the potential of organic farming in India. 
• **Export Potential:** Organic products from India are exported to countries like **USA, Germany, France, and Switzerland**, highlighting the global demand for such produce. 
• **Cluster-Based Approach:** MOVCDNER focuses on cluster formation to achieve economies of scale and better resource management. 
• **North Eastern Region:** Known for its rich biodiversity, unique agro-climatic conditions, and indigenous crop varieties, making it ideal for organic farming. 
• **Certification:** Organic certification is mandatory for farmers under MOVCDNER to ensure credibility and market acceptance of their produce.

questions.question: Volleyball was introduced in the Asian Games in _________ for Men.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1958**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Volleyball** was introduced in the **Asian Games** for men for the first time in the year **1958**.
 
• The **1958 Asian Games**, officially known as the Third Asian Games, were held in **Tokyo, Japan**, from May 24 to June 1, 1958.
 
• Volleyball became an official event for men during these games, marking its debut in the Asian Games history.
 
• In the **1958 Asian Games**, Japan emerged as one of the strongest teams in volleyball, showcasing the sport's growing popularity in the region.
 
• The inclusion of volleyball in the Asian Games demonstrated a significant step in promoting the sport in Asia and elevating its competitive level on an international platform.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Volleyball as a Sport:**

 
 
• Volleyball was invented in **1895** by **William G. Morgan** in the United States as an indoor sport blending elements of basketball, baseball, tennis, and handball.
 
• The sport was designed to be less physically intense than basketball, making it suitable for older members of the YMCA community.
 
• Volleyball is played by two teams of six players each on a rectangular court divided by a net. The objective is to score points by grounding the ball on the opponent's court under organized rules.
 
 
 
• **Asian Games Overview:**
 
 
• The **Asian Games**, also known as the **Asiad**, is a continental multi-sport event held every four years among athletes from all over Asia.
 
• The first Asian Games were held in **1951** in **New Delhi, India**, and featured 11 nations participating in six sports.
 
• Volleyball, as a team sport, was introduced later in **1958**, reflecting the growing importance of team sports in the Asian Games.
 
 
 
• **Other Key Sports Introduced in the Asian Games:**
 
 
• Many sports were gradually included in the Asian Games, such as basketball in **1951**, and football, which has been a part of the games since the inaugural event in 1951.
 
• Team sports like volleyball, basketball, and hockey have played a significant role in enhancing the competitive spirit of the Asian Games.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Volleyball in Asia:**
 
 
• Volleyball is extremely popular in several Asian countries, including **Japan, China, South Korea, and Iran**.
 
• The inclusion of volleyball in the Asian Games provided a platform for Asian teams to compete at a high level and prepare for global events like the Olympics and World Championships.
 
• Countries like **Japan** and **China** have historically dominated volleyball in Asia, securing numerous medals in both men's and women's categories.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Volleyball in the Olympics:** Volleyball became an official Olympic sport in **1964** during the Tokyo Olympics, further cementing its global appeal.
 
• **Asian Volleyball Confederation (AVC):** The **AVC**, established in **1952**, governs volleyball in Asia and organizes tournaments such as the Asian Volleyball Championship.
 
• **Notable Achievements:** Japan's men's and women's volleyball teams have consistently been among the best in Asia, with the men's team winning the gold medal in the **1972 Munich Olympics**.
 
• **Growth of Volleyball:** The sport has witnessed significant growth in popularity due to initiatives like the Asian Games and international tournaments, inspiring millions of athletes across the continent.

questions.question: Who is the author of the book 'The White Tiger'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aravind Adiga**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Aravind Adiga** is the author of the novel **'The White Tiger'**, published in the year **2008**.

• The book **'The White Tiger'** won the prestigious **Man Booker Prize** in the same year, making Adiga one of the youngest authors to receive this honor.

• The novel is a satirical narrative that explores themes of **poverty, corruption, and social inequality** in India.

• The story is told through the perspective of the protagonist, **Balram Halwai**, who rises from a poor background to become a successful entrepreneur in modern India.

• Aravind Adiga was born in **Madras (now Chennai), India**, in **1974**, and he grew up in both India and Australia, which influenced his global perspective.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **About the Novel:**

• The novel is set against the backdrop of **India's economic rise** and highlights the stark contrast between the lives of the rich and the poor.

• The protagonist, Balram Halwai, narrates his journey from being a servant to committing a murder and rising to wealth, symbolizing the struggles of the underprivileged in India.

• The book employs a darkly humorous tone to critique the **caste system and systemic corruption**.

• **Man Booker Prize:**

• The **Man Booker Prize** is one of the most prestigious literary awards given annually for the best original novel written in the English language.

• Aravind Adiga was just **33 years old** when he won this award, making him one of the youngest recipients.

• **Adaptation:**

• **'The White Tiger'** was adapted into a critically acclaimed Netflix film in **2021**, directed by **Ramin Bahrani**.

• The film starred **Adarsh Gourav**, **Priyanka Chopra Jonas**, and **Rajkummar Rao** and received an **Academy Award nomination** for Best Adapted Screenplay.

• **Other Works by Aravind Adiga:**

• Some of Adiga's other notable works include **'Between the Assassinations'** (2008), **'Last Man in Tower'** (2011), and **'Selection Day'** (2016).

• These novels also explore themes of social and economic disparities in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Other Authors Mentioned:**

• **Vikram Seth:** Known for his epic novel **'A Suitable Boy'**, which is one of the longest novels ever published in English.

• **Amitav Ghosh:** A prominent Indian author known for works like **'The Shadow Lines'** and **'The Glass Palace'**.

• **Rohinton Mistry:** A Canadian-Indian author famous for **'A Fine Balance'**, which also explores socio-economic issues in India.

• **Global Recognition of Indian Literature:**

• Indian authors have consistently garnered international acclaim for their works that delve into themes of culture, history, and social issues.

• Other Indian authors who have won the **Man Booker Prize** include **Salman Rushdie** for **'Midnight's Children'** and **Kiran Desai** for **'The Inheritance of Loss'**.

questions.question: Which art form developed as a result of the fusion of Greek and Indian artistic styles?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gandhara art**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Gandhara art** is an ancient art form that developed as a result of the **fusion of Greek and Indian artistic styles**. It flourished during the reign of the Kushan Empire (1st to 5th century CE). 
• This style emerged in the **Gandhara region**, which is located in present-day **northwest Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan**. 
• The hallmark of Gandhara art is its depiction of **Buddhist themes**, especially the life events of Buddha, with a strong influence of **Hellenistic (Greek) artistic techniques**. 
• The art is characterized by **realistic representations** of human figures, intricate detailing, and the use of **grey schist stone**. 
• Key features include the depiction of **Greco-Roman drapery**, curly hair, and facial expressions inspired by Greek sculptures, blended with Indian symbolism and spiritual themes. 
• Important examples of Gandhara art include **Buddha statues**, friezes depicting Jataka tales, and reliefs from monasteries like those in **Taxila** and **Takht-i-Bahi**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Other Indian Artistic Styles:** 
• **Mathura art:** Originating from Mathura (Uttar Pradesh), this art style is characterized by indigenous features and primarily depicts Buddha in a **spiritual and Indianized form**. Unlike Gandhara art, it has minimal external influence. 
• **Amaravati sculpture:** Flourished in the Amaravati region (Andhra Pradesh) under the **Satavahana dynasty**. It is known for its **narrative panels**, intricate carvings, and the use of white marble. It primarily focuses on **Buddhist stupas**. 
• **Gupta art:** Flourished during the Gupta Empire (4th to 6th century CE). It represents the **classical phase of Indian art**, with an emphasis on **graceful figures**, spiritual expressions, and simplified forms. It is considered the **golden age of Indian art**. 
• **Key Features of Gandhara Art:** 
• Extensive use of **Greek techniques**, such as realistic anatomy and drapery folds. 
• Depictions of **Buddha in human form**, which marked a significant shift from earlier aniconic representations. 
• Motifs like **Corinthian columns, vine scrolls, and cherubs** borrowed from Greek architecture. 
• Use of materials like **schist stone**, which allowed for detailed carvings. 
• **Significance of Gandhara Art:** 
• Played a crucial role in the **spread of Buddhism** across Asia, particularly to Central Asia, China, and Japan. 
• Represents a unique example of **cultural syncretism** between East and West. 
• Serves as a historical record of the interaction between **Greek, Roman, and Indian civilizations**. 
• **Modern Relevance:** 
• Archaeological sites in the Gandhara region are now **UNESCO World Heritage Sites**, attracting scholars and tourists globally. 
• The study of Gandhara art helps us understand the **historical trade and cultural exchanges** along the Silk Road. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Key Sites:** Major Gandhara art sites include **Taxila, Bamiyan, Peshawar, and Swat Valley**. These areas were important centers of Buddhist learning and artistic production. 
• **Historical Influence:** The art developed under the patronage of the **Kushan rulers**, especially **Kanishka the Great**, who embraced Buddhism and supported its artistic expression. 
• **Legacy:** Gandhara art laid the foundation for Buddhist art forms in **China, Korea, and Japan**, influencing their cultural and artistic traditions. </ul

questions.question: A girl with 50 kg mass climbs up a rope through a height of 5 metres. She takes 25 s to accomplish the task. What is the power (in watts) expended by the girl?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

• **Work Done (W)**: The girl climbs up a rope through a height of 5 meters. The work done is calculated using the formula: **Work Done (W) = m × g × h**, where:

• **m** is the mass of the girl = **50 kg**.

• **g** is the acceleration due to gravity = **9.8 m/s²**.

• **h** is the height climbed = **5 m**.

Substituting the values: **W = 50 × 9.8 × 5 = 2450 Joules.**

• **Power (P)**: Power is the rate at which work is done. It is calculated using the formula: **P = W / t**, where:

• **W** is the work done = **2450 Joules**.

• **t** is the time taken = 25

questions.question: In May 2025, scientists have created the first 'pangenome' of which crop, an important staple food in Asia?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rice**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• In **May 2025**, scientists successfully created the first-ever **'pangenome' of Rice**, which marks a significant milestone in agricultural genomics. 
• **Rice** is a vital staple food, particularly in **Asia**, where it constitutes a major part of the daily diet for billions of people. 
• A **'pangenome'** represents the complete set of genes found across multiple varieties of a species, providing a comprehensive genetic blueprint for enhancing crop yield, disease resistance, and adaptability. 
• The creation of the rice pangenome is expected to help breeders and researchers develop **climate-resilient rice varieties** and improve food security in the face of global challenges such as climate change. 
• This breakthrough highlights the importance of rice as a global food crop and the role of advanced genomic research in ensuring sustainable agricultural practices. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **What is a Pangenome?** 
• A **Pangenome** is the collection of all the genes present in different varieties or populations of a species, including core genes (common across all varieties) and accessory genes (unique to specific varieties). 
• Pangenomes help researchers identify genetic diversity, allowing for targeted improvements in crop traits such as yield, disease resistance, and environmental adaptability. 
• **Importance of Rice:** 
• Rice is a staple food for more than **50% of the world's population**, particularly in **Asia**, where countries like India, China, and Japan are among the largest producers and consumers. 
• It provides essential **carbohydrates** and is a primary source of nutrition in many developing countries. 
• Rice farming supports the livelihoods of millions of farmers worldwide, making it a critical agricultural commodity. 
• **Other Crops:** 
• **Maize:** A staple food and feed crop widely grown in **North America, Africa, and South America**. It is used for food, animal feed, and industrial applications. 
• **Barley:** Primarily cultivated in **Europe and North America**, barley is used for malting, food, and fodder purposes. 
• **Wheat:** A key cereal crop grown in **temperate regions** globally, it is a major ingredient in bread, pasta, and other food products. 
• **Significance of Genomic Research in Agriculture:** 
• Advanced genomic studies, like the creation of pangenomes, enable the identification of genetic traits that improve crop performance and resilience. 
• These developments are crucial in addressing challenges such as **climate change, pest outbreaks, and increasing global food demand**. 
• They also support the development of sustainable agricultural practices, ensuring long-term food security. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Rice Production in Asia:** 
• Asia accounts for over **90% of global rice production**, with countries like **India, China, Indonesia, and Thailand** being major producers. 
• Rice cultivation is heavily dependent on **irrigation and monsoon rainfall**, making it sensitive to climate change impacts. 
• **Applications of Pangenomics:** 
• Pangenomics aids in identifying **genetic markers** for desirable traits, accelerating the breeding process. 
• It provides insights into the evolutionary history and genetic diversity of species, supporting conservation efforts. 
• In agriculture, pangenomics enables the development of crops with enhanced **nutritional value, stress tolerance, and disease resistance**. 
• **Future Prospects:** 
• Genomic advancements like pangenomics can revolutionize agriculture by addressing challenges such as **food security and climate resilience**. 
• They pave the way for precision agriculture, allowing farmers to optimize crop production based on genetic insights. </ul

questions.question: As of July 2025, the Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited holds which of the following CPSE status?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Miniratna-I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL)** holds the **Miniratna-I status** under the categorization of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) as of **July 2025**.

• **Miniratna-I CPSEs** are granted greater autonomy and financial powers compared to Miniratna-II and other lower-ranked CPSEs. This includes powers to make investments and enter joint ventures.

• BSNL was established on **1st October 2000**, and it is one of the largest telecommunications companies in India, operating under the ownership of the **Department of Telecommunications (DoT), Government of India**.

• The **Miniratna-I status** allows BSNL to approve investments up to **₹500 crore** without requiring approval from the government, provided such investments are within its approved budget.

• BSNL does not hold the **Maharatna** or **Navratna** status, which are granted to CPSEs that demonstrate higher financial performance and strategic importance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Classification of CPSEs:** 

• **Maharatna:** This is the highest status for CPSEs, given to companies with a turnover exceeding ₹25,000 crore, net profit of ₹5,000 crore for three consecutive years, and a significant global presence. Example: ONGC, NTPC.

• **Navratna:** This status is granted to CPSEs that have a minimum score of 60 based on performance parameters like net profit, total manpower cost, and productivity. Example: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL).

• **Miniratna-I:** CPSEs with a positive net worth and a profit for the last three years can qualify as Miniratna-I. They are granted financial autonomy up to ₹500 crore. Example: BSNL, Airports Authority of India.

• **Miniratna-II:** CPSEs with a smaller operational scale than Miniratna-I but meeting profitability criteria for the last three years are classified as Miniratna-II. Example: Bharat Pumps and Compressors Limited.

• **BSNL's Role in Indian Telecom:** 

• BSNL is a major provider of **landline, mobile, broadband, and optical fiber services** across India.

• It serves both urban and rural areas, contributing significantly to **digital inclusivity** in the country.

• BSNL plays a critical role in implementing government initiatives like **BharatNet**, aimed at providing high-speed internet in rural India.

• **Key Features of CPSE Autonomy:** 

• Autonomy is classified into financial and operational categories, allowing CPSEs to make independent decisions within defined limits.

• Higher autonomy enables CPSEs to improve efficiency, innovate, and compete globally.

• Miniratna-I CPSEs can enter joint ventures and approve capital expenditure without prior approval from the government.

• **Important Legislation:** 

• The **Department of Public Enterprises**, under the Ministry of Heavy Industries, oversees CPSE classification and status allocation.

• The autonomy and financial powers granted to CPSEs are defined under specific government guidelines aimed at enhancing their operational performance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Government Guidelines:** 

• CPSE classification is reviewed periodically to ensure alignment with economic and strategic goals.

• Maharatna and Navratna CPSEs are allowed to invest beyond ₹500 crore, reflecting their larger operational scale.

• **BSNL's Strategic Importance:** 

• BSNL is a critical player in ensuring connectivity in remote and rural areas, advancing the government's **Digital India** initiative.

• It also supports national security by maintaining communication infrastructure for government and defense purposes.

questions.question: Who was the chairman of the Tax Reforms Committee 1991?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Raja J. Chelliah**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Raja J. Chelliah** was the chairman of the **Tax Reforms Committee in 1991**, which was constituted by the Government of India to recommend reforms in the taxation system.
 
• The committee was pivotal in shaping India's modern tax policies, focusing on **direct and indirect taxation reforms**.
 
• It aimed to **simplify the tax structure**, broaden the tax base, and improve compliance to boost revenue collection.
 
• The recommendations of the committee included **reducing tax rates, eliminating exemptions, and introducing VAT (Value Added Tax)**.
 
• Raja J. Chelliah is often regarded as the "Father of Tax Reforms" in India due to his significant contributions to the country's fiscal policies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Tax Reforms Committee (1991):**

 
 
• This committee was formed as part of the economic reforms initiated by **Manmohan Singh**, the then Finance Minister under the leadership of Prime Minister **P.V. Narasimha Rao**.
 
• The primary objective was to align India's tax system with the requirements of a modern and liberalized economy.
 
• The committee's work significantly influenced the introduction of **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** years later.
 
 
 
• **Raja J. Chelliah:**
 
 
• He was a renowned Indian economist and a pioneer in the field of public finance and taxation.
 
• He played a crucial role in restructuring India's tax system during the economic reforms of the 1990s.
 
• Chelliah founded the **National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP)**, which continues to play a key role in shaping India's fiscal policies.
 
 
 
• **Key Recommendations of the Tax Reforms Committee:**
 
 
• Reduction of **corporate and personal income tax rates** to encourage compliance.
 
• Introduction of a **moderate and uniform indirect tax system**.
 
• Focus on eliminating tax exemptions and broadening the tax base to enhance revenue.
 
• Adoption of a **modern tax administration system** to reduce evasion and improve efficiency.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Committee's Recommendations:**
 
 
• The recommendations laid the foundation for India's shift toward a market-oriented economy.
 
• Many of the reforms proposed by the committee were implemented in subsequent budgets, leading to a **more transparent and efficient tax system**.
 
• The reforms contributed to **higher tax revenue** and better compliance over time.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Manmohan Singh:** He was the Finance Minister in 1991 and played a crucial role in initiating the **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization (LPG) reforms** in India. However, he was not the chairman of the Tax Reforms Committee.
 
• **P. Chidambaram:** He served as Finance Minister in later years but did not lead the Tax Reforms Committee in 1991.
 
• **Shakti Kant Das:** He is a former Economic Affairs Secretary and currently serves as the Governor of the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**. He was not associated with the Tax Reforms Committee of 1991.
 
• The Tax Reforms Committee under Raja J. Chelliah's chairmanship remains a landmark in India's fiscal history, driving substantial changes in the country's tax landscape.

[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** • **Mangal Pandey**, a soldier in the **34th Bengal Native Infantry** of the British East India Company, was a key figure in the events leading to the Indian Rebellion of 1857. • Mangal Pandey attacked British officers on **March 29, 1857**, at the military garrison of **Barrackpore** near Kolkata (then Calcutta). • He was subsequently court-martialed and sentenced to death for his actions of rebellion and insubordination. • **Barrackpore**, a town in West Bengal, served as a major military cantonment under the British rule, and it was the location of this significant incident. • Mangal Pandey was hanged to death on **April 8, 1857**, at Barrackpore, making him one of the earliest martyrs of the Indian freedom struggle.

questions.question: A majority of the total membership of the House and a majority of not less than _________ of the members present and voting is required for adoption of effective clauses and motions for consideration and passing of Constitution Amendment Bills.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• A **Constitution Amendment Bill** in India requires a **special majority** for its adoption in the Parliament. 
• This special majority is defined as a **majority of the total membership of the House** and a **majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting**. 
• **Article 368** of the **Indian Constitution** deals with the procedure for amending the Constitution, including the requirement for this special majority. 
• The **total membership** of the House refers to the total strength of the House, irrespective of vacancies or absentees. 
• The inclusion of **"members present and voting"** excludes those who abstain from voting or are absent during the voting process. 
• The dates in the incorrect options (Options 1, 3, 4, and 5) are irrelevant to the context of passing Constitution Amendment Bills. Hence, the **correct answer is Option 2**, which aligns with the legal requirements for a Constitution Amendment Bill under Article 368. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Types of Majority:** 
• **Simple Majority:** Refers to a majority of members present and voting. It is used for ordinary bills and certain motions. 
• **Absolute Majority:** Refers to a majority of the total membership of the House, regardless of whether members are present or absent. 
• **Effective Majority:** Refers to a majority of the total membership of the House, excluding vacancies. 
• **Special Majority:** Used for amending the Constitution. Requires a majority of the total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting. 
• **Procedure for Amending the Constitution:** 
• A Constitution Amendment Bill can be introduced in either House of Parliament, not necessarily on the recommendation of the President. 
• The Bill must be passed by a **special majority** in both Houses of Parliament (as defined under Article 368). 
• In some cases, the Bill also needs to be ratified by at least half of the **State Legislatures** (e.g., for changes in federal provisions). 
• Once passed, the Bill is sent to the President for assent. The President cannot withhold assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill. 
• **Articles Related to Constitutional Amendments:** 
• **Article 368:** Lays down the procedure for amending the Constitution. 
• **Article 4:** Deals with laws made under Articles 2 and 3, which may include provisions for amending the Constitution without following the Article 368 procedure. 
• **Examples of Constitutional Amendments:** 
• **42nd Amendment (1976):** Known as the "Mini-Constitution," it brought extensive changes to the Constitution. 
• **73rd Amendment (1992):** Introduced the Panchayati Raj system in India. 
• **101st Amendment (2016):** Introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST). 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• The **special majority** under Article 368 ensures that significant changes to the Constitution have widespread support and cannot be passed easily by a simple majority. 
• In cases where a **federal feature** is affected (e.g., altering the distribution of powers between the Union and States), ratification by at least half of the **State Legislatures** is necessary. 
• Not all amendments require a **special majority**; for example, amendments made under Articles 2 and 3 (related to the reorganization of states) are exceptions. 
• As of 2023, there have been **105 constitutional amendments**, demonstrating the evolving nature of the Indian Constitution to address changing societal and political needs. </ul
